Blanchefleur.json.text: Blanchefleur is an Arthurian heroine. She is also called Blancheflor. The knight Percival entered the land of the wounded Fisher King. There he found the fair woman and asked for her hand. Her name means white flower. In some texts the name belongs to Percival's sister. That sister is otherwise known as Dindraine.

Blaí.json.text: Blaí is an Irish heroine. She is the mother of Oisín, the poet of the band called the Fianna. A magical enemy turned her into a deer. She bore her son while in that deer shape. Fionn Mac Cumhaill fathered the boy. Her son entered life in human shape. Blaí was warned not to touch him. She still stroked him with her tongue. A small furry patch stayed on his brow. The heroine often carries the name Sadb.

Blodeuwedd.json.text: Blodeuwedd is a Welsh goddess. Her name means flower face. The white maiden Arianrhod bore a son after a trick. She then cursed the boy. He could not hold a name, weapons, or a wife. Her brother Gwydion tricked her again. He won a name and a weapon for the young. Gwydion crafted a wife with the magician Math. In the fourth branch of the Mabinogion they worked this feat. They shaped Blodeuwedd from nine wildflowers. Among those plants were meadowsweet and oak, then broom, primrose, and cockle.

Blondine.json.text: Blondine is a heroine of Brittany. She appears in a folktale of that land. The tale is rich with myth signs. Some readers name her a fallen goddess. A youth called Cado mocked a fairy. The fairy then cast a spell. Only a princess could break that spell. She was called Blondine. No man could guide Cado to her land. He heard crows speaking about her. They told him the way. Cado rode on the back of a crow. The bird led him to Blondine. She waited by a good well. Cado took her from her wizard father. The father fired weak spells as they ran. On the earth Cado broke his promise. He lost the ring she had pressed on him. He forgot her completely. He planned to wed another. Blondine came to that wedding in her ring. Cado then recalled his true bride. The two were wed at last.

Blue_Men_of_the_Minch.json.text: The Blue Men of the Minch are Scottish folkloric figures. They are also called Fir Gorm and Fir Ghorma. The channel of the Minch divides the Hebrides. Blue-skinned beings haunt the coastal water. They may come from seals. They may be fallen angels. The Blue Men rule the weather of the channel. They rule the ships that cross it too.

Bláthnat.json.text: Bláthnat is an Irish goddess. Her name means little flower. A tale names her the daughter of Midir. Midir was the king of the Irish fairies. Another tale says she was the child of Ulster's ruler. That ruler was Concobar Mac Nessa. The hero Cúchulainn carried Bláthnat from the Otherworld. He carried her magic cattle and a cauldron too. His comrade in that raid was Cú Roí. Cú Roí then stole the cattle and the cauldron. Cú Roí also buried the maiden. She did not live well beside Cú Roí. She planned his murder within a year. Bláthnat took the hero Cúchulainn as her lover. She told him the secret to kill her husband. This makes her the Irish form of the Welsh Blodeuwedd. Cú Roí's poet Fercheertne pushed her over a cliff. He died in the same act. She later chose the forgiven life of a nun.

Bochtóg.json.text: Bochtóg is an Irish heroine. A fairy woman saved people from drowning. She woke sleepers on the shore as the tide rose. That wakeful act saved them from the sea. She was seen in rough weather. When visible she was a beautiful woman. Her waist-length hair was blonde.

Bodb_Derg.json.text: Bodb Derg is an Irish god or hero. He was the strongest magician of the Tuatha Dé Danann. He was the son of the good god Dagda. He was also the brother of Aonghus Óg, the god of poetry. He ruled from a great palace on the edge of Lough Derg. The Tuatha Dé elected him king. That choice angered the god Lir. Bodb Derg then punished Aífe. She had enchanted the children of Lir into swans. He turned Aífe into a demon or a crane.
